In [[statistics]], a '''variational series''' is a non-decreasing sequence <math>X_{(1)} \leqslant X_{(2)} \leqslant \cdots \leqslant X_{(n-1)} \leqslant X_{(n)}</math>composed from an initial series of [[independent and identically distributed random variables]] <math>X_1,\ldots,X_n</math>. The members of the variational series form [[order statistics]], which form the basis for [[Nonparametric statistics|nonparametric statistical methods]].

<math>X_{(k)}</math> is called the ''k''th order statistic, while the values <math> X_{(1)}=\min_{1 \leq k \leq n}{X_k}</math> and <math> X_{(n)}=\max_{1 \leq k \leq n}{X_k} </math> (the 1st and <math>n</math>th order statistics, respectively) are referred to as the extremal terms.<ref name="shalyt">{{cite web |last1=Shalyt |first1=A.I. |title=Variational series |url=http://www.encyclopediaofmath.org/index.php?title=Variational_series&oldid=14157 |website=Encyclopedia of Mathematics |accessdate=14 February 2020 |date=7 February 2011}}</ref> The [[Range (statistics)|sample range]] is given by <math>R_n = X_{(n)}-X_{(1)}</math>,<ref name="shalyt" /> and the [[Median#Medians for samples|sample median]] by <math>X_{(m+1)}</math> when <math>n=2m+1</math> is odd and <math>(X_{(m+1)} + X_{(m)})/2</math> when <math>n=2m</math> is even.

The variational series serves to construct the [[empirical distribution function]] <math>\hat{F}(x) = \mu(x)/n</math> , where <math> \mu(x) </math> is the number of members of the series which are less than <math>x</math>.  The empirical distribution <math>\hat{F}(x)</math> serves as an estimate of the true distribution <math>F(x)</math> of the random variables<math>X_1,\ldots,X_n</math>, and according to the [[Glivenko–Cantelli theorem]] converges [[Convergence of random variables#Almost sure convergence|almost surely]] to <math>F(x)</math>.
